images.alt: A Commodore PET 2001 computer, a sheet-metal trapezoid with built-in monitor, chiclet keyboard and cassette deck, photographed from the front
images.caption: Screen, keyboard, cassette deck and computer sealed into one metal case — in 1977 nothing else you could buy arrived like this.

images.alt: A Commodore PET 2001 computer shown at an angle, with its monitor, chiclet keyboard and built-in cassette deck visible
images.caption: Chuck Peddle's argument to Jack Tramiel was that Commodore should sell a whole computer, not just the 6502 chip inside it.

images.alt: Close-up view of the built-in cassette recorder on the front panel of a Commodore PET 2001
images.caption: The cassette deck was built into the case itself — no recorder to buy separately, no cables to wire up.

images.alt: Close-up view of the calculator-style chiclet keyboard and numeric keypad on a Commodore PET 2001
images.caption: The PET's calculator-style chiclet keys were disliked from the start; Commodore replaced them with a full-travel keyboard in 1979.

images.alt: A Commodore PET 2001 computer photographed from the front, showing its integrated monitor, keyboard and cassette deck
images.caption: The PET's character set and screen-poking habits carried on into the VIC-20 and Commodore 64, machines that sold in the millions.
